items.caption:
Check out the Voxel Butler robot... Could be yours in 2028 for roughly $20k.

(New video edit test - Gave Clause ungraded S-Log footage and had it color grade as part of the editing workflow)
items.transcript: This is the coolest thing I saw today. This is a Voxel, and it's basically a little droid robot thing that walks around your house and cleans up after you. It's from a New York company called Tuesday Labs. The founder used to work on Spot's arm at Boston Dynamics. And then in their launch video, they literally put up a card that says, this is not CGI. So here it is sweeping crumbs into a little dustpan, and here it's watering a bonsai tree. And if you lose your phone, you can just ask it where it last saw it. Now, the funny thing is they work with a former Pixar character designer and animators actually made 3D animations of how it should move before they even built it. And then they train the robot on those moves, which is probably why it looks like it moves a bit like a cartoon character. And in my favorite demo, he hands this guy a clarinet and then sort of like dances along as he plays it, which is kind of adorable actually. But they're estimating it'll cost about $20,000. It's not shipping until 2028. And right now it's using a combination of both AI and sometimes a human actually controlling it. So the first set of owners are basically helping to train the future versions. I don't know, 20 grand is kind of expensive, but I wouldn't mind having one of these follow me around and clean up after me. Would you pay 20K for one?

items.transcript: Here are three useful prompts to use with ChatGPT's new agents. They're called DOTs. They're always on AI agents that can use their own computer and your connected apps to get things done in the background. One, track my recent purchases for price drops, check refund policies, and draft price adjustment requests for me to approve. So if something you bought gets cheaper, your DOT can help you get some money back. Two, monitor my upcoming flights, and if it gets delayed or I miss my connection, find alternative routes and compare costs. That way, your DOT has a backup plan just in case of a travel disaster. Three, check my email and calendar for commitments I've made and remind me before they're due. Never forget something you've promised you would do. Unlike a normal chat GPT prompt, your DOT keeps working on these responsibilities without you having to constantly remind it. So if you want to check it out, more info is in the caption.

items.caption:
Kimi K3.1 Pro appears to be nearly as good as the big lab state of the art models... And it's open-weight! So wild!

#kimi #openweight #aimodels
items.transcript: This is the craziest thing I've seen today. This new AI model made all of these video games and well, technically you're gonna be able to download this model for free. This is Kimi K 3.1 Pro from Chinese Lab Moonshot AI. And they're saying it built all of these demos on its own in actual game engines like Unity and Unreal. So like this racing game and this zombie shooter and this parkour game where you're ziplining across roofs for some reason. And it even built this entire medieval town inside of Blender. And the reason this is a big deal is because this is an open model, but it's also basically almost as good as all of the state-of-the-art closed models. Artificial analysis has it ranked fourth out of all of the models that it tests. And on one of the big coding benchmarks, it's less than one point behind Opus 5.5 from Anthropic. But it's literally half the price of Opus and like one-fifth the price of GPT-6 Astra. And then on November 4th, they're releasing the full model. So theoretically, any company can download the model and run it on their own servers. I mean, if you've got enough compute, which it needs a lot. Quite honestly, the gap between the free models and the big lab paid models is really closing quickly. So I'm curious, would you switch and use one of these Chinese models if it was just as good as the state of the art labs?

items.caption:
Your smartphone can be the brain of your next robot.

Fun fact: this was the first video where I let AI do the entire edit for me. I just recorded me talking and Claude found the b-roll, edited the footage, added the subtitles, and everything in-between. How did Claude do?
items.transcript: This is the coolest thing I saw today. Somebody turned a cheap old smartphone into the brain of a walking robot. It's called PhoneBot, and it comes out of Dennis Hong's robotics lab at UCLA. The phone isn't a remote. The phone is the robot. Its camera is the eyes, its motion sensors handles the balance, and the AI that makes it walk runs right on the phone. They trained that AI in a simulation first, and the early versions literally walked with a limp. Then they loaded it onto a real phone and, well, here it is walking around a living room. But here's the best part. Lay it flat on its face and it just gets back up all by itself. The phones they use, they cost like 50 to 80 bucks. Now, the body is about 400 bucks, but similar research humanoids cost anywhere from $3,500 all the way up to 14 grand. And they're open sourcing all of it. The parts list, the 3D print files, everything. Now it's tiny and it has no arms yet, but it can already follow you around and film you. The Unitree Kung-Fu Legend Robot Looks Insane! This, once again, is NOT AI!

#Robots #robotics @unitree__robotics
items.transcript: All right, this is the craziest thing I've seen today. This is the Unitree H2X Kung Fu Legend Robot. And the footage you're seeing is all in real time. This isn't sped up. This robot is meant for personal defense. Here we can see it beating the crap out of a car from different angles, really showing that car who's boss, jumping off a four meter high platform, doing like ninja spin kicks. Like this looks like it could mess you up and it can stand for up to eight hours. Here it is with fire coming out of its foot for some reason. And we can see it here being used for personal protection when an invader tries to break into somebody's house with a knife. Yeah, I would want to mess with that thing. And in one of the coolest demos, it's actually lifting a car up so it can rescue someone from underneath. And here it is rescuing a child from almost being hit by a car. Now, I haven't been able to find any more information, about that specific robot, but it's a pretty impressive demo. What could possibly go wrong in the future?
